title: Alert warning time
prompt: The alert service promises to warn people well before bad weather starts. Write `solve(weather_alerts)` so it returns `alert_id`, `alert_type`, `warning_minutes` and `start_weekday`.
rules: `warning_minutes` is the time from `issued_at` to `starts_at` in whole minutes, as an int. A part minute is dropped: 119 minutes 30 seconds is 119.
`start_weekday` is the full English name of the day `starts_at` falls on, such as `Monday`. All times are UTC.
A missing time gives missing results. Return the four columns, in that order, for every alert.
hints: Cast each timestamp to `long` to get seconds; their difference is the warning in seconds.
Divide by 60 for minutes, then cast to `int`: the cast drops the part minute.
`F.date_format(col, pattern)` writes a day's name. `EEE` gives the short name; `EEEE` gives the full one.
starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F


def solve(weather_alerts):
    # Return alert_id, alert_type, warning_minutes and start_weekday.
    return weather_alerts
explanation: Casting a timestamp to `long` gives seconds since 1970, so `F.col("starts_at").cast("long") - F.col("issued_at").cast("long")` is the warning in seconds. `/ 60` gives minutes as a `double`, and `.cast("int")` drops the part minute. The day name is `F.date_format("starts_at", "EEEE")`. Together: `weather_alerts.select("alert_id", "alert_type", ((seconds) / 60).cast("int").alias("warning_minutes"), F.date_format("starts_at", "EEEE").alias("start_weekday"))`. Working from the clock parts instead, such as `hour * 60 + minute` of each time, breaks as soon as an alert is issued before midnight and starts after it. `F.dayofweek` gives a number, not a name.
